loText: Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.
question: A junior risk analyst at a Shanghai life insurer is preparing an induction slide on performance measurement for newly hired analysts. The slide defines the excess return of an asset or strategy as $\text{r}^{\text{x}}_{\text{t}} = \text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}$, and she wants to add one accompanying statement. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.A: Excess returns are called active returns because producing the benchmark return itself requires investment knowledge and continuous human intervention.
options.B: The benchmark return $\text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}$ must come from a single published market index, since a combination of assets or asset classes cannot serve as a benchmark.
options.C: The benchmark return $\text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}$ is by definition the risk-free rate, so every excess return in this equation is measured against the T-bill return.
options.D: Calling excess returns active returns presumes that the benchmark is passive and can be produced without investment knowledge, for example through a low-cost index fund.

solution:
Induction slide on $\text{r}^{\text{x}}_{\text{t}} = \text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}$: which accompanying statement about excess (active) return is most accurate?

Alpha cannot be defined until a benchmark is defined, so the starting object is the excess return. GARP (Equation 3.1) defines it period by period:

$\text{r}^{\text{x}}_{\text{t}} = \text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}$,

where $\text{r}_{\text{t}}$ is the return of the asset or strategy in period t and $\text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}$ is the benchmark return for the same period. question:
A treasury analyst at a Canadian university endowment is calculating the alpha of an external Canadian equity manager against its benchmark, the S&P/TSX Composite Index, over the last six months. Monthly returns are shown below.

| Month | Fund return (%) | Benchmark return (%) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1.40 | 1.10 |
| 2 | −0.60 | −0.90 |
| 3 | 2.10 | 1.50 |
| 4 | 0.80 | 0.95 |
| 5 | −1.20 | −1.65 |
| 6 | 1.90 | 1.30 |

Assets under management are CAD 850 million and the average one-month T-bill rate over the period was 0.30% per month. The endowment annualises a monthly average return by multiplying it by 12. What is the manager’s annualised alpha?
solution:
Six months of fund and S&P/TSX returns, with AUM and a T-bill rate given: annualised alpha using the ×12 convention.

**Concept and theory**

GARP defines alpha as “the average return in excess of a benchmark.” With T observations of the excess return (Equation 3.1), Equation 3.2 is the sample mean:

Two points follow. First, alpha is a mean, so it is computed from the benchmark the mandate defines; any other rate in the data (here the T-bill rate) is irrelevant unless it is the benchmark. Second, alpha is an average return, so it scales with time linearly: GARP annualises Berkshire  […]

question:
A risk committee member at a Hong Kong family office is reviewing a manager’s pitch book, which states: “Our alpha of 3.1% per year proves our skill.” She drafts four comments for the committee:

I. Alpha is first and foremost a statement about the benchmark against which it is measured, so the pitch must state that benchmark.

II. Alpha by itself could be produced by taking large amounts of risk, which is why it should be divided by the tracking error.

III. Because alpha is the average excess return over the sample, a positive alpha is sufficient evidence of manager skill.

IV. Alpha is the standard deviation of the manager’s excess returns, so the 3.1% figure also measures the manager’s active risk.

Which of the comments are consistent with the definition and interpretation of alpha?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I and III only
options.C: II and IV only
options.D: I, II and III only

solution:
Pitch claims a 3.1% alpha “proves skill”: which of four committee comments are consistent with the definition and interpretation of alpha?

**Concept and theory**

GARP opens Section 3.3 with a warning: “Alpha is often interpreted as a measure of skill. That is debatable. It is first and foremost a statement about a benchmark.” Alpha is computed as the average excess return over a benchmark (Equation 3.2); change the benchmark and the alpha changes. That is why the benchmark must always be stated with the alpha.

| X | 18.0 | 1.2 | 3.0 |
| Y | 15.0 | 2.4 | 6.0 |
| Z | 22.0 | 0.9 | 4.5 |

question:
A senior risk analyst at a Tokyo trust bank is calculating the information ratio of a Japanese equity fund benchmarked to the TOPIX. Annual returns over five years are shown below.

| Year | Fund return (%) | TOPIX return (%) | Risk-free rate (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8.0 | 6.5 | 0.5 |
| 2 | −3.0 | −4.0 | 0.5 |
| 3 | 12.5 | 10.0 | 0.5 |
| 4 | 6.0 | 7.0 | 0.5 |
| 5 | 1.5 | 0.5 | 0.5 |

Using the sample standard deviation (divide by T − 1), which of the following is closest to the fund’s information ratio against the TOPIX?

question:

| P | 1.8 | 2.0 |
| Q | 4.2 | 7.0 |
| R | 3.0 | 2.5 |
| S | 0.9 | 1.2 |

question:
A junior analyst at a US charitable foundation is comparing two funds using the Sharpe ratio. Annualised data over the same sample:

| Item | Fund K (%) | Fund L (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Mean return | 9.4 | 7.6 |
| Volatility of returns | 14.0 | 8.0 |
| Tracking error versus the Russell 1000 | 5.0 | 4.0 |

Over the sample, the Russell 1000 returned 8.0% per year on average and one-month T-bills averaged 2.0% per year. Which of the following pairs gives the Sharpe ratios of Fund K and Fund L, respectively?
solution:
Two US funds with mean returns, volatilities and tracking errors, plus the Russell 1000 return and the T-bill rate: Sharpe ratios of K and L.

**Concept and theory**

GARP presents the Sharpe ratio as a special case of the information ratio: when the benchmark is the risk-free rate $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ , alpha is the average return in excess of $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ and the information ratio coincides with the Sharpe ratio:

$$\text{SR} = \frac{\overline{\text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}}}}{\sigma},$$

where the bar denotes the sample average of the excess return over the risk-free rate and $\sigma$ is the volatility of the asset. Schweser: “This measure has alpha in the numerator and the standard deviation of the asset in the denominator.”

question: A risk consultant advising a Brazilian pension fund, which treats the short-term BRL deposit rate as its risk-free rate, is writing a methodology note on computing Sharpe ratios for its managers. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

In the Sharpe ratio, the benchmark is the risk-free rate. GARP adds two technical facts:

1. Timing: “the risk-free rate is known at the beginning of the period and applies from t − 1 to t.” A T-bill or deposit bought at t − 1 locks in its return for the period, unlike the risky asset whose return is learned only at t.
2. Volatility: footnote 2, “In practice, volatilities of excess returns or raw returns are generally almost the same, unless risk-free rates are very volatile, which happens in some emerging markets.”

question: A senior risk analyst at a Singapore asset manager is presenting Grinold’s fundamental law of active management to newly hired analysts. She wants one slide that states what the law says and why its output carries a particular label. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.A: The law gives the information ratio a manager will realize after transactions costs and trading restrictions, provided its IC and BR inputs are estimated without error.
options.B: The law formalizes the idea that a manager creates alpha by keeping holdings close to the benchmark, so that the most successful bets are the smallest deviations from it.
options.C: The law gives the maximum attainable information ratio, IR $= \text{IC} \times\sqrt{\text{BR}}$, because it ignores transactions costs, restrictions on trading and other real-world considerations.
options.D: The law holds as an exact identity, so a manager who achieves the stated IC and BR is assured of earning the resulting information ratio in every year.

solution:
Senior risk analyst at a Singapore asset manager: which statement best states what Grinold’s law says and why its output is labeled as it is?

**Concept and theory**

A portfolio manager creates alpha relative to a benchmark by making bets that deviate from that benchmark; the more successful the bets, the higher the alpha. Grinold (1989) made this intuition formal. The fundamental law links the information ratio (IR, alpha per unit of tracking error) to two properties of the manager’s process:

IR $= \text{IC} \times\sqrt{\text{BR}}$,

II. Breadth reflects both the number of securities that can be traded and how frequently they can be traded.

loText: Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.
question:
A member of the risk committee at a UK life insurer is comparing two equity managers using the fundamental law. Manager P runs a concentrated macro timing strategy; Manager Q runs a quantitative cross-sectional strategy that combines value and momentum signals.

| Manager | Independent bets per year | IC | Mandate size |
|---|---|---|---|
| P | 9 | 0.200 | GBP 300 million |
| Q | 576 | 0.025 | GBP 300 million |

Which of the following statements best describes the comparison under the law?

options.A: Both have a law-implied IR of 0.60: P plays well with narrow breadth while Q plays often with a small edge, and the law treats both routes to a high IR as valid.
options.B: Both have a law-implied IR of 0.60, but Q’s much larger breadth shows that Q is the more skillful forecaster of the two, so Q should be preferred.
options.C: P’s law-implied IR exceeds Q’s, because placing only nine bets a year reduces the chance of making mistakes and so raises expected performance.
options.D: Only P reaches an IR of 0.60, because under the law an IC as small as 0.025 cannot produce a useful information ratio, whatever the breadth.

solution:
UK insurer risk committee: comparing a 9-bet macro timer (IC 0.20) with a 576-bet value and momentum manager (IC 0.025).

**Concept and theory**

The law shows a central trade-off in active management. Grinold and Kahn put it as: it is important “to play often (high breadth, BR) and to play well (high IC)”. GARP sums up: you can be very talented at forecasting and make few bets really count, or you can have a very small edge but make a lot of bets, and both lead to high information ratios. Cross-sectional strategies such as value, size and momentum have great breadth because hundreds of stocks can be traded, so ICs of 2% to 5% can be highly profitable. IC is the skill measure; BR is a count of independent opportunities, not a measure of skill.

Which of the following statements in the memo is NOT correct?

options.A: The law is derived under mean-variance utility, so the shortcomings of mean-variance utility also apply to it.
options.B: The framework assumes that all of the information available to the manager is used optimally.
options.C: The framework ignores higher-moment risks such as skewness, but it does capture downside risk because the IR scales alpha by tracking error.
options.D: The relationship IR $= \text{IC} \times\sqrt{\text{BR}}$ is itself an approximation within the mean-variance framework.

solution:
Australian superannuation fund model validation: which memo statement about the law’s assumptions is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP states the law’s assumptions in one compact passage:

- It is derived under mean-variance utility, so all the shortcomings of mean-variance utility apply.
- In particular, using mean-variance utility, the framework ignores downside risk and other higher-moment risk, while assuming that all information is used optimally.
- A crucial assumption is that the forecasts are independent of each other.
- Footnote 3: the law is itself an approximation in the mean-variance framework; better approximations and extensions exist.

question: The chief risk officer of a German insurer is reviewing a proposal for a EUR overlay mandate. The manager sells out-of-the-money equity index put options on many separate underlyings, collecting premiums in most months but facing occasional large losses. Using an estimated IC and the number of independent positions, the manager’s pitch shows a law-implied information ratio well above 1.0. Which concern about this use of the law is most directly grounded in the law’s own assumptions?

options.A: The law penalizes left-tail losses through the IC term, so the high IR shown in the pitch already reflects the occasional large losses.
options.B: The law is derived under mean-variance utility and ignores downside and higher-moment risk, so a high IR can overstate the appeal of a strategy with rare large losses.
options.C: Transactions costs on the options are understated, since the law builds these costs into the maximum information ratio it reports.
options.D: ICs fall as assets under management rise, and the law captures this by reducing the breadth input as the overlay grows.

solution:
German insurer CRO: a put-selling overlay pitched with a law-implied IR above 1.0; which concern rests on the law’s own assumptions?

**Concept and theory**

The law is built on mean-variance utility. Mean-variance preferences rank strategies by mean and variance only. A strategy that sells out-of-the-money puts earns small, steady premiums most of the time and suffers rare, large losses: its return distribution is negatively skewed with a fat left tail. Variance (and hence tracking error and IR) understates how unpleasant those rare losses are (an explanatory gloss on the source). GARP states that, by using mean-variance utility, the framework ignores downside risk and other higher-moment risk. A law-implied IR therefore cannot be read as evidence that such a strategy is attractive.

loText: Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.
question: A board member of a US university endowment is reviewing a proposal from the investment office. The flagship active equity program has an IC of 0.08 on 100 independent bets per year. The office proposes to grow the program’s assets from USD 0.5 billion to USD 5 billion by hiring additional external sub-managers, raising breadth to 400 independent bets per year. Due diligence confirms that the new sub-managers’ forecasts are uncorrelated with each other and with the existing bets. The office projects an information ratio of 1.60. Which of the following statements best evaluates the projection?

options.A: The projection is conservative, because a larger program can fund more research, which raises the IC above 0.08 and lifts the IR beyond 1.60.
options.B: The projection is sound, because IC and BR are properties of the strategy itself, and neither input is affected by the size of the program.
options.C: The projection understates the IR, because quadrupling breadth should quadruple the IR to 3.20 when the IC stays at 0.08.
options.D: The projection is likely overstated, because it assumes the IC stays at 0.08 across the added breadth, whereas ICs tend to fall as hiring widens and assets rise.

solution:
US endowment board member: program grows from USD 0.5bn to USD 5bn, breadth from 100 to 400 uncorrelated bets, IR projected at 1.60.

**Concept and theory**

GARP names two very important limitations of the fundamental law. The first: ICs are assumed to be constant across BR. “The first manager whom you find may truly have a high IC, but the one hundredth manager whom you hire probably does not.” As assets under management increase, the ability to generate ICs diminishes. The empirical evidence shows decreasing returns to scale: as funds get bigger, performance deteriorates, in mutual funds, hedge funds and private equity. Thus ICs tend to fall as AUM rise. (The second limitation, correlated bets reducing BR, is ruled out in this stem by the due-diligence finding.)

question: A senior risk analyst at a Chinese life insurer is reviewing a CNY fixed income manager-of-managers program. The program has hired 40 external bond managers; each was asked to beat its benchmark, and each has done so by buying illiquid, higher-yielding corporate bonds. The program’s annual report applies the fundamental law with breadth set equal to the total number of bond positions held across all 40 managers. Which statement best describes the problem with the report?

options.A: Because all 40 managers are reaching for yield, the program holds essentially a single bet on an illiquidity factor rather than many independent bets, so breadth and the IR are overstated.
options.B: Hiring 40 separate managers ensures that their forecasts are independent of each other, so the report’s breadth is correct and the IR it shows is reliable.
options.C: The common illiquidity exposure lowers each manager’s IC but leaves breadth unchanged, so only the IC input in the report needs to be revised.
options.D: Correlated forecasts matter for equity factor tilts such as value against growth, but not for bond portfolios, so the report’s breadth can stand.

solution:
Chinese life insurer: 40 bond managers all reaching for yield in illiquid bonds; report sets BR equal to total positions.

**Concept and theory**

The law’s crucial assumption is that forecasts are independent of each other. GARP’s second limitation: it is difficult to have truly independent forecasts in BR. Manager decisions tend to be correlated, and correlated bets reduce BR. GARP gives two illustrations:

- An equity manager overweight 1,000 value stocks and underweight 1,000 growth stocks has not placed 1,000 different bets, but just one bet on a value-growth factor.
- Hiring one hundred fixed income managers who are all “reaching for yield” by buying illiquid bonds gives not one hundred different bets but a single bet on an illiquidity factor.

question: A risk consultant is preparing a briefing for the board of a Dutch pension fund on what Grinold’s fundamental law can and cannot do for the fund’s EUR active equity program. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.A: The law appears widely in the academic literature, because it links the information ratio to the economic sources of risk premiums.
options.B: The law identifies where positive risk-adjusted opportunities lie, so it serves chiefly as a tool for searching out high-IR strategies.
options.C: Under the law’s framing, alpha requires superior information; a superior ability to process public information is not enough to generate it.

solution:
Risk consultant’s board briefing: what the law can and cannot do; which statement is most accurate?

GARP is explicit about the nature of the law:

- The law is useful to frame the active management process: alpha begins with raw information, which is processed into forecasts, and then portfolios are constructed optimally to balance return forecasts against risk.
- The key to generating alpha is forecasting, which requires superior information or superior ability to process public information.

solution:
Asian pension trustee studying NBIM under Knut Kjær: how did NBIM apply the law?

Since alpha is created by finding many different forecasts that are independent, the law suggests seeking breadth through independence. The law takes IC as constant across BR, but GARP’s first limitation is that this is unrealistic: as assets under management increase, the ability to generate ICs diminishes, and the evidence on active management shows decreasing returns to scale.
